rows.a:
Deferral is the founding concept of Center Study: the act that, on the originary scene, turned a rush toward a shared object into the first sign. A group converges on something everyone wants, the old pecking order collapses, and someone's grasping hand slows into a gesture that points at the object instead of seizing it. Others imitate that gesture, and violence is held off. Katz insists on the word because its near synonyms ("postpone," "prevent," "refrain from") all imply a finished decision made from outside the situation. Deferral, he says, "keeps us always inside the scene, so that knowledge of the scene is always a part of concern for sustaining the scene" ([Lecture 3: Deferral of Violence](/post/deferral-of-violence#p-8)). We can't even know exactly what was deferred, because no one knows what would have happened without the sign.

Deferral also has no expiration date. In Katz's words, "unlike, e.g., 'prevent,' 'refrain from,' 'desist,' and other near synonyms, 'deferral' posits no endpoint. As long as there is humanity there is deferral" ([Deferral, Debt and the Idiom](/post/deferral-debt-and-the-idiom#p-1)). It differs from deterrence because it allows "an orderly distribution": we don't just watch each other warily, we share.

Deferral is not mere self-denial. Katz anticipates the objection that you eventually have to eat or hit back, and answers that "the effect is of a new world opening up" ([The Generativity of Deferral](/post/the-generativity-of-deferral#p-1)). Every time you hold back from the obvious move, new possibilities appear: rivals become collaborators, and a quarrel can become a joke. Institutions are scaled-up deferrals. Ritual, law, credit, manners and sovereignty are all ways of keeping the rush to the center at a distance. Even a hasty "excuse me" in a crowded hallway defers a small conflict and continues an institution of politeness.

Read next: [Lecture 3: Deferral of Violence](/post/deferral-of-violence). It works through why the word matters, and what it means that we have "never left" the originary scene.

rows.a:
For Katz, an idiom is any use of language as it actually lives: "a singular use of language, meaningful in its particular and always changing uses" ([Infra-Humaning](/post/infra-humaning#p-7)). He chose the word deliberately to replace "theory" and "metalanguage." Disciplines tend to claim a privileged language that stands above ordinary speech and judges it. "Idiom" refuses that claim. There is no neutral vantage outside language, and "the highest knowledge is to know that you are always in an idiom because there is nothing but idioms" ([Idiomatic Intelligence as Register](/post/idiomatic-intelligence-as-register#p-14)). That is why he can say the originary hypothesis itself is "the idiomaticity of idioms": on the originary scene, the participants invented a shared way of pointing that they all had to learn on the spot.

An idiom is not just a vocabulary. It is a pattern of speech forms tied to scenes. Katz describes it as "particular set of ostensive-imperative-interrogative-declarative sequences, so learning an idiom is learning when, for example, someone asking a question or making a statement is really requesting that you do something" ([Scenic/Event Intelligence](/post/scenic-event-intelligence#p-13)). To learn an idiom, then, is to learn its implicit commands and what it points to, not only its words.

Idioms are also made, and the making is close to everyday conversation. Keeping a conversation alive involves "the perpetual recycling of words used earlier so as to turn them into reference points that can frame the conversation itself. An idiom is that, sustained indefinitely" ([Programming the Same](/post/programming-the-same#p-27)). This is why Katz keeps coining phrases such as "donate your resentment to the center." Each one is a reference point meant to circulate. It is also why he values moving between idioms. You learn one well enough that its boundary with another idiom shows, and then you make both idioms "speak about themselves."

For a next step, read [Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining). It is his most sustained attempt to make "idiom" do real work, as an alternative both to "cognition" and to "viral" theories of language.

rows.a:
The Big Man is the figure in Center Study who first puts a human being where only the sacred object had stood. The term comes from the anthropologist Marshall Sahlins by way of Eric Gans. In the egalitarian community that follows the originary scene, the center is held by a shared object of desire and ritual: an animal, an ancestor. The Big Man, acting on what Gans calls "producer's desire," disciplines himself, accumulates and out-gives everyone else until no one can repay him. In Katz's words, he places himself "beyond any possible reciprocal gift relation" ([Anthropomorphics and Reaction](/post/anthropomorphics-and-reaction#p-5)). He now occupies the center and becomes the source of distribution.

Katz treats this as the decisive revolution after the originary event itself: "The Big Man is the beginning of history and of all our ethical and political dilemmas" ([What is to be Undone?, 1](/post/what-is-to-be-undone-1#p-7)). Two things follow. Hierarchy and inequality enter for good. And resentment, which was once directed at the withholding central object, now settles on a man. That man has to manage rivals, settle disputes and be seen to do it well, and keep down those who dream of returning to equality. Katz is clear that the usurpation is not mere appetite: "if the Big Man were just acting on his own desire for centrality, he would have no idea what to do once he acquired it" ([Power and Paradox](/post/power-and-paradox-pdf#p-25)). He resolves a crisis among contenders.

From here Katz traces a line through chiefdom, sacral kingship and divine emperors down to presidents and bosses. One consequence matters especially for him: "Once the center has been humanly occupied, it must remain humanly occupied" ([Sacral Kingship and After](/post/sacral-kingship-and-after-preliminary-reflections#p-2)). This is why so much of his later work concerns succession. Modern politics, in his view, is largely a matter of taking sides for or against the Big Man revolution, and he defends it.

To read next: [Anthropomorphics and Reaction](/post/anthropomorphics-and-reaction). It sets out the Big Man's emergence and his problems with rivals, and follows the figure through to the question of secure sovereignty today.

rows.q: Why does Katz say there is no economy?
rows.a:
Katz's claim is that the "economy," imagined as a self-standing domain of self-interested individuals trading, with politics and culture added on top, is an ideological picture laid over something older and more basic: our debt to the center. In the originary scene the central object gives itself to be shared, and the community owes the center in return. Everything we call economic is a later elaboration of that exchange. In his words: "There is no “economy.” There is only, as there always has been, ritual distribution from the center" ([Will Have Been the Same](/post/will-have-been-the-same-future-perfectism-or-derivatives-of-the-tributary#p-1)).

The historical argument supports this. Barter did not grow into markets and money by itself. "Markets do not spring up spontaneously out of an evolving division of labor... Markets are created by states" ([Center and Distribution](/post/anthropomorphics-center-and-distribution#p-2)). They were set up to provision soldiers, and money was issued by a central authority, partly so that people could pay what they owed to the center. Seen from this angle, what we call the economy is the layered pattern of distribution and delegation that flows outward from whoever occupies the center: "The “economy” is just everyone’s place, and everyone’s seeking to (re)place, in the order of having distributed to one and that one distributing to others" ([The Transfer Idiom](/post/the-transfer-idiom#p-11)). Money marks how far one stands from that center.

The claim also looks forward. If the real substance is debt to the center, then an order organized around emulation and succession, rather than "self-interest," "would no longer be an economy, but what we might call a 'tributary' order, in which our originary debt to the center is acknowledged and paid" ([There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-95)). Katz is not saying exchange is unreal. He is saying that treating it as autonomous hides who distributes and who enforces.

Read next: [There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf), written with Zack Baker. It works the argument through money, central banking, derivatives and succession.

rows.a:
Not in the ordinary sense, but Katz would say the question is harder than it looks. Writing about Generative Anthropology, the field Center Study grows out of, he grants that "GA is not a faith or religion, and, of course, they are right—in a way it is the antithesis of faith and religion by disclosing the originary possibility of all faiths and religions" ([Originary Hypothesis as Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-1)). The originary hypothesis holds that language, the human and the sacred begin together, in a single gesture that defers violence around a shared center. That gives it an account of where every religion comes from, which is a different thing from being one more religion.

It also does not stand outside faith as a secular debunker would. Katz insists that "the faiths are truer than philosophy, and it's not even close." He describes Center Study's odd position as "a perfectly materialist refutation of materialism, the one true faith masquerading as subversive heresy" ([same text](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip#p-2)). It cuts the traditional divine out of the account, but "in place of the divine or holy we have the center which can never quite be 'human' yet governs all" ([Tagging and Tracking the Human](/post/tagging-and-tracking-the-human#p-5)).

So the religious vocabulary is not simply thrown away. It is translated. Words like "spirituality," "religion" and "faith," Katz says, "refer to hypotheses I consider defunct. I have consistently proposed replacing them with language" ([Nomos and Transfer Translation](/post/nomos-and-transfer-translation#p-12)). His point is that every act of speech, every naming and promise, re-enacts the originary gesture that founded the sacred. Existing faiths can therefore be read as particular discoveries of that origin. They are not refuted, but they are not the last word either. Center Study treats them, as it treats every discipline, as scenes to be entered and studied, "a kind of center study" in their own right ([Secular Thinking](/post/secular-thinking#p-21)).

Read next: [Originary Hypothesis as Mobius Strip](/post/originary-hypothesis-as-mobius-strip). It works through exactly this ambivalence, including why taking the hypothesis seriously can feel like a conversion.

rows.q: How would Center Study read a social media pile-on?
rows.a:
For Center Study a pile-on is a small model of the mimetic crisis: attention converges on one figure, and each new participant joins because others already have. Katz uses exactly this example to define the center: "The center is whatever interferes with violent centralization." He asks whether you have ever felt the urge to "pile on" someone, and notes that "there is no way you would have been thinking of the clever bon mot you are about to add without the mimetic instigation of those who have already dropped a couple" ([Revivalistics](/post/revivalistics#p-1)). The pile-on is *violent centralization*: the target is made the center, and he is made a target rather than a source of deferral.

The harder question Katz raises in the same paragraph is where the line falls. We have to be allowed "sharp and uncompromising critiques," even the punishment of criminals, or we could not oppose scapegoating without doing it ourselves. The difference is not how severe the criticism is. It is whether attention ends in a sign that defers violence or in the ritual expulsion of a victim.

He does not take this to mean that social media is simply a machine for scapegoating. "A lot of scapegoating takes place on social media," he concedes, but its better use is "to design social interactions or 'interfaces' that foreground dangerous markings along with ways of deferring their danger" ([Design and the Attentional Economy](/post/design-and-the-attentional-economy#p-14)). For someone caught inside a pile-on, the practical lesson is in his account of the exemplary victim: avoid taking up "the posture of the exemplary victim in waiting," which says that by rejecting me you put yourself on History's wrong side ([Lecture 4: The Center](/post/the-center#p-19)). Do not double down, and do not counter-accuse. Name what the crowd is converging on, so that the scene can find another center.

To read next, try [Lecture 4: The Center](/post/the-center). It sets out how the exemplary victim became the modern template for being a center, and why that template keeps producing pile-ons.
